books.section: Topic 3.12 Movement in the Early Republic

stimulus.text: Paraphrase: From the 1600s into the 1790s, backcountry farmers repeatedly clashed with coastal elites. In 1676, Virginia backcountry settlers rose in Bacon’s Rebellion, saying they paid heavy taxes, had little voice in the legislature, and got no protection from Native attacks. In the 1760s, Carolina backcountry farmers formed the Regulator movement against merchants, courts, and sheriffs they called corrupt, and fought the War of the Regulation in 1771. In 1763–1764, the Paxton Boys of western Pennsylvania attacked Native settlements and defied the colonial government. In 1786–1787, debt-burdened farmers in western Massachusetts rose in Shays’s Rebellion against taxes and courts that seized their land for debt.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase drawn from Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.12.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.12.
stem: Why did backcountry farmers and coastal elites keep clashing, even after independence?

options.text: Because the backcountry wanted to rejoin Britain and the coast refused.
options.misconception: Background: after independence, backcountry farmers did not seek a return to British rule.

options.text: Because coastal elites banned all settlement west of the mountains.
options.misconception: Background: no such ban existed after independence; settlers poured west.

options.text: Because the backcountry had no farms and the coast had no ports.
options.misconception: Background: the backcountry farmed and the coast traded; each had its own economy.

options.text: Because the two groups lived by different economies and wanted different things.

rationales.A: Background: independence was settled; the backcountry did not seek British rule again.
rationales.B: Background: settlement westward grew after independence; no ban blocked it.
rationales.C: Background: each region had its own working economy: farms inland, trade on the coast.
rationales.D: Background: backcountry farmers wanted cheap land, protection, and easy credit, while coastal merchants and officials wanted taxes paid, debts collected, and order kept. Their interests pulled apart.
rationales.general:
1. Background: backcountry life ran on farming, land, and credit from local merchants.
2. Background: coastal life ran on trade, banks, and taxes that paid public debts.
3. Background: a government that pleased one side pinched the other: collecting debts helped creditors and crushed debtors.
4. So the clash came from different ways of making a living, not from one bad law.
Remember: when two groups want opposite things from the same government, expect repeated conflict.
